Fidget toys, but make them cool and executive. Seriously: the silver design and the sleek gift box make this the perfect gift for your favorite corporate office-dweller.

Your man deserves to be comfy cozy too, and he’ll love these snuggly woven Uggs for your date nights in.

This very loud, compact, and waterproof speaker is completely worth the money. It's so waterproof that Hannah Oh's still worked perfectly after being left outside in the sun and pouring rain for a week.

#6754. The Scoop with RBO’s Sophie Wybrew-Bond: On Their Festive Partnership with L’Oréal Paris

Welcome to the Scoop: a weekly email series in which I quiz fashion insiders on the stories of the week. This will be a way for the Vogue Business community to synthesize and reflect on the latest headlines and get a little inside scoop every Friday.

This week’s guest is the Royal Ballet and Opera’s chief commercial officer, Sophie Wybrew-Bond. After a career in media, Sophie joined the Royal Opera House in 2024, as the organization looked to build a more resilient mixed-funding model.

One of the first things Sophie did was to add the word ‘ballet’ to the name. Ballet is half of what the company does, but according to Sophie, 30% of their audience didn’t know it. They do now — and they have grown as well. In the years since Covid, the RBO’s social channels have grown from about 3 million followers to 7.5 million, mostly because they began posting content that felt light and organic, rather than branded.

At the same time, much like everywhere else in culture, brand partners at the Royal Ballet and Opera House are arguably more important than ever. I called up Sophie to find out their plans for the festive season.

This year’s festive partner for the Royal Ballet and Opera is L’Oréal Paris. This is the second time we have had a Christmas partner — last year’s was Paul Smith. L’Oréal Paris is designing the Christmas tree in the Paul Hamlyn Hall. The concept we are working with is “Where beauty meets performance”.

We want a tree of discovery; meaning that people come into the house and even if they don’t have a ticket, they’ll spend a bit of time looking and finding details and delightful extra bits that you don’t notice at first glance. We’ve got 10 bespoke dioramas, which are like little storytelling elements to the tree, which then have L’Oréal Paris products within them. At the top of the tree, we’ve got a star made of pointe shoes that glitter. We will be unveiling the tree next Wednesday, November 18.

We actually also announced a beauty partnership with L’Oréal Parisjust recently, which means their product is being used by our wigs, hair and makeup teams. One of our principals, Marianela Nunez, who’s been with the company for 26 years, is the face of that partnership. As part of that, we offer some behind-the-scenes tours to our community. We program moments during the holidays, where you can drink and dine or listen to music — and it will be all around the tree. Because of The Nutcracker, people will be coming into the house to feel festive.

Christmas tree ornaments composed of L’Oréal Paris products.

How did the partnership with L’Oréal Paris happen?

It’s really important for us that partnerships are not like a badge-type sponsorship. The storytelling on digital channels is as important. While thousands of people will see this tree, hundreds of thousands more will see it on digital channels across the world. The impact that we had with our Paul Smith partnership last year was pretty visible so L’Oréal Paris came to us to explore working together.

I was interviewing Sydney Levrone last week at the Vogue Business Global Summit. She spoke about the relationship between sport and beauty, and how all the track and field athletes these days are “completely glammed out”.

Certainly, the Royal Ballet dancers are elite athletes and then they need to have an artistic interpretation on top of the technique and the athleticism they exhibit. It sets the bar really high on both sides. So when it comes to beauty, you need to make sure you have a partner who meets those standards with high performance products. The product needs to last through really extreme circumstances, which is why we came up with that “beauty meets performance” theme.

Behind the scenes for the festive preparations at Royal Ballet & Opera.

How closely do you follow fashion? And why is it important for ballet to be connected to the fashion and luxury industries?

In our case, we’re very, very interested in how fashion houses are telling their stories. But fashion and ballet have always been quite closely connected. Obviously, costumes have to be aesthetically beautiful, but they also have to perform. They have to work with choreography, they have to allow movement and breathing, but also hold their shape in this high-performance environment. As fashion has had such an evolution in terms of textile and cut and the way things move, it’s easy to see the common threads all the way through.

We have worked with so many brands and designers, including Erdem, Daniel Lee at Burberry, Roksanda, Saul Nash and Gareth Pugh.

It’s been almost a year since Timothée Chalamet said no one cares about ballet and opera any more. Yet, as we reported, we have seen a tremendous interest on fashion’s side for ballet this year. Is there a connection between the two — did the comments lead to a renewed interest in ballet?

Not at all. There is a news cycle which obviously has peaks and troughs. And then there is perennial shared storytelling. I think what happened with those comments is that they spiked in the news cycle at that point in time, but the relationship between fashion and ballet is always there. Timothée Chalamet’s comments provoked a reaction and so kickstarted a news cycle, which we were able to use for more storytelling on social media and the overwhelming positive response was just brilliant.

Podcasts are having a moment. Do you guys have one?

Right now, we’re in the cinema, on socials and on YouTube. I want us to be part of whatever the conversation is, and to do that we need to be on channels and in formats where people aren’t expecting to see us. It’s not about selling tickets but about having the Royal Ballet and Opera perceived as exciting and relevant, even if they are only following us on social media. I am developing some audio products. Watch this space. There’ll be another scoop.

#6753. What Does Transgender Mean? Everything You Need to Know, According to Experts

From gender identity to transition, here's what the term actually means.

The word "transgender" gets used a lot these days, but that doesn't necessarily indicate that everyone understands what being transgender actually means. Between headlines, social media debates, and ongoing conversations about gender identity, it's easy to feel like you're missing a piece of the puzzle or even worry about using the wrong terminology altogether. Fortunately, understanding what it means to be transgender doesn't have to be as complicated as the internet sometimes makes it seem.

"Being transgender means your gender identity doesn't align with the one you were assigned at birth. That's the whole heart of it," says licensed marriage and family therapist Adrienne Michelle, LMFT. "It doesn't tell you anything about how someone looks, what they've explored medically, or how far along they are in any journey. It's simply about your authentic sense of self being different from what you were told you were at the start."

Ultimately, gender is deeply personal, and there's no one "right" way to be transgender. Whether you're talking with a friend, supporting a loved one, or simply trying to better understand the world around you, having a basic understanding of transgender identity can make the conversation feel a whole lot less intimidating and a lot more inclusive.

The term "transgender" is an identity label that refers to people whose gender identity doesn’t match the sex they were assigned when they were born, explains therapist and LGBTQ+ educator Zoe Stoller. You'll also often hear transgender shortened to simply trans. The prefix trans- means "across" or "on the other side of," reflecting that a person's gender identity differs from the sex they were assigned at birth.

"Gender is expansive, and 'trans' is the umbrella term that often holds all of that expansiveness," says Michelle. "It isn't a single identity; it's a beautifully wide category that makes room for so many people."

The transgender umbrella includes trans men, trans women, and many nonbinary identities, though not everyone whose gender identity differs from the sex they were assigned at birth identifies as transgender. And that's completely okay. The right label is the one that feels right to the person using it.

Although they're often used interchangeably, sex and gender aren't the same thing. Sex refers to the biological characteristics someone is labeled or assigned at birth, while gender refers to a person's internal sense of who they are. You may also come across the terms AFAB/AMAB (assigned female at birth/assigned male at birth), which describe the sex someone was assigned when they were born, not their gender identity. And while babies are often labeled male or female at birth, sex itself isn't always binary, as intersex people exist too.

Once you understand that distinction, a lot of the terminology starts to make more sense. Terms like nonbinary, genderfluid, genderqueer, and gender nonconforming all describe distinct experiences or expressions of gender, but they aren't interchangeable, and they don't all automatically mean someone is transgender. (P.S. If you're looking for a deeper breakdown of those identities, check out our complete gender identity glossary.)

"Gender nonconforming is about not feeling aligned with the normative, performative ways gender is 'supposed' to show up—the expectations around how a man or woman should look, dress, or move through the world," says Michelle. "It's about expression, not identity. You can be gender nonconforming and cisgender, and you can be gender nonconforming and trans. The two sometimes overlap, but they're answering different questions: transgender is about who you are, gender nonconforming is about how you show up."

As Stoller explains, the transgender umbrella includes both binary identities (such as trans men and trans women) and many nonbinary identities, though not everyone whose gender differs from the sex they were assigned at birth identifies as transgender. Like every other aspect of identity, everyone's relationship with gender is unique.

First things first: Despite the headline right above this, there's no one way to "look" transgender.

As Stoller explains, being transgender isn't defined by surgeries, medical procedures, or any other external milestone. The only thing someone needs to "count" as transgender is feeling that the label accurately reflects who they are. For many people, that identity is deeply affirming regardless of whether they ever choose to transition.

Transitioning simply refers to the process of aligning someone's life more closely with their gender identity. "It’s important to note that transition isn't a checklist," says Michelle. "Some people explore hormones or surgery, some focus on legal or social changes, some pursue none of it, and every one of those paths is whole and valid."

Transitioning can look different for everyone, but it's generally broken into a few categories:

Some people choose to align their outward appearance with their gender identity because it's an affirming—and sometimes life-saving—way to feel seen as their authentic selves, Stoller says. Others don't transition at all or may be unable to do so for personal, financial, or safety reasons. Regardless, their gender identity is no less valid.

Now that you know what transgender means, it's worth talking about how to actually use the term. According to Michelle, "transgender" is an adjective, not a noun. "You'd say 'a transgender person' or 'transgender people,' never 'a transgender' or 'the transgenders,'" she explains. "It works just like any other descriptive word; you wouldn't call someone 'a tall,' so the same care applies here."

As Stoller explains, it's also important not to assume someone identifies as transgender unless they've shared that information with you. Even if you think someone's gender identity technically falls under the transgender umbrella, it's ultimately up to them to decide which labels feel the most accurate and affirming. When in doubt, use the language someone uses to describe themselves.

One of the most common terminology mix-ups is the difference between a trans man and a trans woman. "A trans man is someone who was assigned female at birth and now identifies and lives as a man. A trans woman was assigned male at birth and identifies and lives as a woman," explains Michelle.

It's an important distinction because these terms describe who someone is, not who they used to be. In other words, trans men are men, and trans women are women. The word trans simply provides additional context about their gender journey—it doesn't change their gender.

As Stoller notes, some trans men and trans women identify fully within the traditional gender binary, while others may also feel connected to nonbinary experiences. Like every other aspect of gender identity, there's no one "right" way to experience or describe being transgender.

The short answer? Use the pronouns someone asks you to use. It's really that simple.

As Stoller explains, people—whether they're transgender or cisgender—can use whatever pronouns feel the most affirming to them, including multiple sets of pronouns or neopronouns. Although people often associate certain pronouns with certain genders, pronouns don't always tell you someone's gender identity.

If you aren't sure which pronouns someone uses, it's okay to politely ask. And if you accidentally get it wrong, apologize, correct yourself, and move on.

Another common misconception is that being transgender somehow determines who someone is attracted to. It doesn't.

Gender identity and sexual orientation are two completely different things (and both are different from romantic orientation), Michelle explains. Gender identity describes who someone is, while sexual orientation describes who they're attracted to. That means transgender people can be straight, gay, lesbian, bisexual, pansexual, asexual, or identify with any other sexual orientation—just like cisgender people.

Like gender identity, sexuality is deeply personal. Labels can be helpful, Stoller says, but they don't always capture the full picture of someone's experience, so it's always best to use the language someone chooses for themselves.

Being a good LGBTQ ally doesn't require having all the answers. It starts with listening, staying open to learning, and treating transgender people with the same respect you'd want someone to show you.

Use the name and pronouns someone asks you to use, and don't make assumptions based on their appearance or gender identity. As Michelle explains, a trans man might use he/him pronouns, a trans woman might use she/her, and a nonbinary person might use they/them—or another set of pronouns that feels most affirming to them. If you aren't sure, it's okay to politely ask.

You may also come across the word transsexual, particularly in older books, articles, or medical literature. While some transgender people have reclaimed the term for themselves, Stoller notes that it's generally considered more outdated and medicalized than transgender, and many people find it offensive. Unless someone has specifically told you that's the label they use, it's best to avoid it.

Above all, remember that every transgender person's experience is different. Listening, respecting the language people use to describe themselves, and remaining open to learning will go a long way.

If you've made it this far because you're wondering whether the word transgender might describe you, know that you don't have to have everything figured out today. Gender identity isn't a quiz you pass or fail, and there's no deadline for understanding yourself.

As Stoller explains, there's no single way to experience being transgender because every person's relationship with gender is different. Some people transition socially, medically, or legally, while others never transition at all. None of those experiences make someone's identity any more or less real.

If you'd like support, consider talking with an LGBTQIA+-affirming therapist, connecting with trusted friends or loved ones, or exploring resources from organizations like The Trevor Project can be a good place to start. You don't have to navigate questions about your identity alone.

As Michelle puts it, "Gender is expansive, full stop." The most important thing isn't fitting neatly into someone else's definition; it's giving yourself the space to discover what feels authentic to you.

#6752. I Found the Most Comfortable Pointed-Toe Boots

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Buying pointed-toe boots has always been a challenge for me because I’m built like a ballerina—not, sadly, in terms of long legs or elegant arms or a swanlike neck, but in terms of feet. I have the bunions of a woman who has dedicated her life to the art of dance, which is ironic because I took ballet lessons for all of three months when I was eight. (I quit after they let me wear the tutu, which was really the only thing I was in it for.) I am confessing this not because I enjoy talking about my feet on the internet, but to establish my credibility when I say that I have finally found a pair of slim, sexy, pointed-toe boots that are comfortable enough to wear all day, even for those of us with less-than-ideal extremities.

Margaux’s Inga boots have a long, squared-off toe and a little kitten heel that measures 1.5 inches—tall enough to give you a bit of a lift, but low enough to be walkable. They come in black leather and a sleek espresso suede, both of which look great with jeans but would also be cute peeking out of long, drapey trousers. The best part is the sizing: Margaux offers its boots in narrow, medium, and wide, and somehow, through the magic of proportion play, the wide does not look wide. They accommodate the fullest part of my foot without looking bulky or breaking up the nice long line.

The first time I wore them, it was to a witches’ dinner that my friend Mo throws every Halloween. She invites 30 of her best female friends over, decorates her home in high goth style, and serves us a theatrically witchy meal. (This time, it was black squid-ink pasta.) Of course, one has to dress appropriately to dine with the coven, so I paired the boots with slim black jeans and a sheer black polka-dotted top. Not only did I get a bunch of compliments, but I didn’t find myself pining for my broomstick on the walk home—the boots were just as comfortable at the end of the evening as they’d been at the start of the night.

They’ve held up equally well on the commute to work. In addition to the extra width, they also come with five millimeters of cushioning on the inside, which is enough to protect you when you’re pounding the pavement. Ever since slimmer toes reentered the fashion conversation, I’ve been faced with the choice between sitting out the trend or hobbling around in boots that fundamentally do not fit. As much as I love a good pair of shoes, I also live for a long walk, and the Ingas, miraculously, let me have both. Really, they don’t feel like heels at all, which is a rare and wonderful thing for a pair of pointed-toe kitten-heel boots.

#6751. 'Wild Horse Nine' Should Win an Oscar for Its Signet Rings

Wild Horse Nine is a Western. Sort of. Yes, Martin McDonagh’s new film is set on Easter Island (known locally as Rapa Nui) in the Pacific Ocean. And yes, this is the 1970s, with John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell playing CIA operatives who take a break from plotting a coup in Chile to tour the stone moai heads.

But there are also—as the title suggests—a lot of wild horses about, plus a cameo from Tom Waits in a shack in Colorado’s Monument Valley and a hell of a lot of Western accessories. Rockwell’s turquoise belt buckle and cowboy hat almost had me wanting to jump back in time and become a paid-up member of the American deep state. And the big signet rings with chunky stones everyone’s wearing? Look, if you really need me to fictionally assassinate JFK and frame Lee Harvey Oswald for it, I’ll step up.

Costume designer Eimer Ní Mhaoldomhnaigh, who worked with McDonagh on The Banshees of Inisherin, had fun outfitting everyone in colorful shirts and flared trousers. “I really liked the way men dressed in the ’70s,” she says. “There was almost a dandyish quality to them.” But it’s the accessories that really makes the characters. “Anytime you’re doing a fitting [for] a male actor,” she explains, “you’re putting on the shirt and the trousers and they’re like, ‘Mmm, okay.’ Then you put on that belt, you give him a Cuban heel and a cowboy hat and a ring, suddenly they start to stand differently. They get the whole swagger. A costume is never finished until you have all those details.”

This is a film with a lot of those details. Rockwell’s cowboy hat, for example, was custom-made by the London milliner Sophie Lamb, who's worked on films like Phantom Thread. His belt buckle is in the traditional Navajo style of the American West: sterling silver with turquoise inlay, which Mhaoldomhnaigh says she “probably got it on Etsy.” That said, she does a lot of IRL trawling on London’s Portobello Road, too. “I really wanted Sam to wear a chain, but when we put it on with the whole outfit, it felt like overkill—like we were decorating a Christmas tree. You have all those things and then you have to pull back a little bit.”

There’s other great gear in the vein of brash, peacocking men of action. “It’s a very American look,” says Mhaoldomhnaigh. Steve Buscemi, who plays the CIA’s South American boss, is in Coblens glasses with gradated lenses, and a ’70s watch from Rotary. Rockwell has a chunky gold watch from Pierre Jacquard. Malkovich, whose character is still stuck in his ’60s glory days, has this whole pork-pie hat thing happening.

But what really gets me going is the rings. Pretty much everyone—including Waits, who plays Malkovich’s hippie brother—has got these chunky rings on, and of a kind we don’t necessarily associate with gray-suitness of the American establishment today. It’s more dandyish, as Mhaoldomhnaigh puts it: “I was a child in the ’70s,” she says. “I always remember older men wearing those type of rings. My dad had one.”

She was on the lookout for designs which matched her memories, both vintage and new—Malkovich’s ring, which is gold with a black onyx stone, was “actually bought in Liberty,” she says, referring to the famous British department store.

“Martin’s films are always a little bit heightened,” the costume designer says. “That’s part of the fun of it, being able to create these slightly heightened characters.” And dressing up those characters means you can have fun, as McDonagh does, in mocking their big egos. Even so, I’m being deadly serious when I say I’d ransack Mhaoldomhnaigh’s props box any time.

A version of this story originally appeared in British GQ.

#6749. My First Job in Fashion: Renzo Rosso

This story is part of 'My First Job in Fashion', interviews with fashion insiders on the roles who made them who they are today.

My first ever job outside my family’s farm was as a carpenter. Every summer, from the age of 10 until I was 16, I worked for a woodworking company that made kitchen furniture. One summer, they put me with two guys building a dining table — one of those extendable ones where you add a leaf in the middle. Every day I went to work and did exactly the same thing: I was the kid helping two men put together the same table, over and over again.

Within a month, the owner had moved the other two onto a different project and left me to make the tables by myself.

A young Renzo Rosso with his father, Vittorio, and mother Fortunata.

I’ve always had a slightly different way of working; I think a little differently from most people. But I love being part of a team, and I have always looked for people who know the things I don’t. That’s how I worked with John Galliano, for instance. I am not a designer — he is. But we were always in conversation, and together we made Maison Margiela a real success.

I grew up in Brugine, in the countryside not far from Venice, Italy. My parents were farmers, and they wanted at least one of their three children to study. My father decided it should be me. For secondary school, I chose the textile program at the Marconi Technical Institute in Padua — a fashion school — because it was the easiest. I didn’t like studying.

But I loved jeans. Growing up, I wore my brother’s hand-me-downs. Then one day, when I was 12, I saw a pair of jeans at the market and begged my mother to please, please buy them for me. She did, that same day. I felt like a king at school; all the kids admired those jeans. I loved them so much I never took the paper tag off the back pocket. I just wore them to school with the tag on. Something inside me was already calling me to fashion. I just didn’t know it yet.

It was the early 1970s, and you have to understand what that time was like. Kids were really starting to rebel against their parents’ generation. It was the Beatles and the Rolling Stones, marijuana, people throwing away their suits for denim. It was a revolution.

At Marconi, I made my first pair of jeans: low-rise and flared. Then I made more on my mother’s sewing machine and sold them to my friends. That’s also when I had the idea of stone-washing. The denim felt too stiff, so I took a stone and started rubbing the jeans with it to soften them.

Fashion school gave me structure. It taught me patterns, stitching, and how the industry works. But I am not a designer; I am someone with good ideas. I went on to study economics at Ca' Foscari, the University of Venice, but I dropped out in 1976 to take my first real job in fashion.

A friend told me about an opening at a clothing manufacturer called Moltex. I went in for an interview with the owner, Adriano Goldschmied, and told him two things: that I was qualified for the job, and that I had already done my military service, which was mandatory in Italy at the time. Neither was true. I had never worked in fashion, and I was still waiting for my call-up letter. Thank God, it never came.

Adriano hired me as production manager at Moltex, which made trousers for one of his brands, Daily Blue. There were 20 girls working there and huge stacks of denim to get through every day. Luckily, I learn fast. Unluckily, I also liked to party — a lot — and sometimes that got in the way. At one point, Adriano wanted to fire me, but his wife told him to give me a second chance because I was clever and had a winner’s attitude. It’s true: even when I lose, I make sure I learn from my mistakes so I win the next time.

Instead of firing me, Adriano changed my pay structure from a fixed salary to a performance-based one to motivate me, and in a single month, my salary went from 240,000 lira ($137) to 2.4 million lira ($1,375). After that, I worked like crazy. But it didn’t last long: a few months later I quit, because I wanted to start my own brand. Adriano didn’t want to let me go, so he proposed we start Diesel together. We did, in 1978.

Rosso with Adriano Goldschmied in Breganze.

Adriano was very well known in the Italian fashion industry back then, and thanks to him, doors opened for me. I started traveling to trade shows and meeting customers from all over the world — Los Angeles, Helsinki, Stockholm, Berlin, New York, Tokyo. We also bought and launched many other brands, like Replay, King Jeans, Viavai, Hot Product and Martin Guy, and that’s how the Genius Group was born. It was a real education.

I worked day and night on eight different lines, eight different collections. I took care of the product side and made sure everything got delivered, while my partner was in charge of design. Eventually I got tired of working on all those brands, so I sold my stakes in the Genius Group back to Adriano and, in 1985, bought 100% of Diesel.

That’s when I really started doing things my way. It wasn’t easy, but I was so convinced of what Diesel could become that I never gave up. I drove all over Europe with nothing but samples in my bag. Around that time, I also started making jeans from denim scraps. Some stores sent them back, convinced we had made a mistake and shipped them old trousers.

A truck Rosso drove in the early years of Diesel to deliver samples and collections all over Europe.

It took Italy a while to understand Diesel. The 1980s were the Paninari years, and they all wore the same uniform: puffer jackets and Levi’s. My Italian agents begged me to make the collections more commercial. I refused. That’s why Diesel was always more successful abroad than at home. My first wholesale customers were Fred Segal in Los Angeles, Henry Lehr in New York, Mario’s in Seattle, and Riccardi in Boston.

Diesel was one of the first companies with a truly global mindset. The French thought we were French, the Americans thought we were American, the Germans thought we were German. And so on.

I couldn’t find Italians who understood my way of thinking, so I started hiring people I met on the street, in bars, at Studio 54. Wherever I traveled, if I met someone who matched my philosophy, I brought them to Italy to work with me. People with different backgrounds, different education, different religions — and we all spoke English. That’s why the product was global from day one.

Opening of a Diesel store in Milan in the late ’90s.

The first Diesel store opened in 1996 in Lexington, New York.

I could go on for hours. I could talk about the crazy graphic designer I met in London who ended up creating the Diesel “Only the Brave” logo with the metropolitan punk, or the countless campaigns we dreamt up. There’s just so much to cover.

A documentary on the story of my life called Be Brave, directed by Francesco Carrozzini, was recently presented at the Venice International Film Festival, and I have just finished working on my biography written by Simone Marchetti of Vanity Fair Italy. Reading it back reminded me how much I’ve done in my life. I’m proud of it, of course. But what surprises me most is how many people I’ve met along the way. The people are the best part.

#6746. Get Huge’s Director on How Looksmaxxing Is a ‘Trap’ for Men

Chasing physical perfection is a hobby now. This year, the community of men obsessed with climbing the ranks of society via square jawlines and hunter eyes, became a subject of widespread fascination. Once a term known in niche internet forums in the early 2010s, the concept of “looksmaxxing” has gone mainstream. These days, even the casual scrollers among us have probably heard of techniques like bonesmashing and mewing.

But beyond a few self-appointed figureheads of the movement, the question of who is buying into these extreme self-improvement measures has loomed large. In Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death documentarian Stacey Lee gives viewers a deeper look into the lives of some of the looksmaxxing community’s more controversial figures. The three-part Hulu docuseries, out now, follows bodybuilding and biohacking influencer Dr. Tony Huge (whose real name is Anthony Hughes), controversial fitness personality, Connor Murphy, and a handful of other men.

Set largely in Thailand, the series tells the story of how these influencers decamped abroad and continued to post near daily videos of their body modification techniques. Lee also confronts the disturbing pattern of deaths among Huge’s inner circle, some of which have gone unsolved. Ultimately the series raises larger questions about the cultural, gender-driven motivations to push the limits of their bodies. GQ spoke with Lee about her nearly two-year immersion into a small corner of this community, the blurred lines between online persona and reality, and what it all reveals about a generation of young men who are seemingly searching for identity, connection, and purpose through increasingly unhealthy outlets.

These internet influencers create so much content, and there's a performance of masculinity that takes place within it. The topic is incredibly polarizing, but also very nuanced. We wanted to capture this world in a way that was more dimensional than what YouTube feeds allow, puncturing the veneer of performance to show who these people are beyond their online personas. I want audiences to see a more multifaceted view of this world and decide for themselves how they feel about these characters based on what they're seeing.

Looksmaxxing wasn't even a term when we started this project [in 2024]. We initially entered the bodybuilding, biohacking, and masculinity influencer community, which was still very fringe at the time. Tony had started making content nearly a decade ago, using shock value and radical transparency to build his brand. He was willing to do things on camera that others wouldn't, challenging social taboos. Ten years later, we're seeing a new generation of influencers who grew up watching Tony, [biohacking YouTuber Leo and Longevity], and Connor and are now using similar methods. But the algorithm has shifted the goalposts significantly since 2016, pushing the content into a much more extreme and nihilistic space.

I wouldn't necessarily say he was the godfather of looksmaxxing, but he was certainly influential in the biohacking and bodybuilding space. Connor Murphy was probably more directly connected to the origins of looksmaxxing, and Clavicular has referenced him as an inspiration. Tony was part of that same world, but represented a different generation.

Tony was a larger-than-life figure, but it was also a broader cultural moment. Around 2016, we were seeing the first Trump presidency, the post-Me Too movement, and the rise of Red Pill philosophy. There were several figures galvanizing these ideas, and Tony was among them.

I think what you're also referring to is this idea of legacy, right? He created something he believed was his unique gift to the world, but there's a sense that the next generation doesn't recognize him or understand his influence. That disconnect seems to drive some of his pursuit of the next big thing, which, in this instance, is looksmaxxing.

Look, Tony is incredibly charismatic and easygoing. Honestly, filming with him was a really respectful process. I think at times it was really discombobulating because he's always smiling in these videos, and he's presenting as this happy-go-lucky kind of guy, but then you're stopped in your tracks because he's doing and saying things that run against that.

The only other reference I'm thinking of is Andrew Tate, who presents in this very sinister way and has a darkness to him that's front and center. Tony doesn't present that way. For us, it was important to show that and to dimensionalize him. In his eyes, he didn't care if he was a hero or a villain. He just wanted to get his story out there. My approach was that I wanted to humanize him, but it wasn't about excusing what was happening.

It's important in this day and age to approach controversial subjects with an element of humanity while still maintaining journalistic independence. In this world, the boundaries are really slippery because people are performing so much. You really have to have your guard up about what's real and what's not. I don't think it's my job to tell audiences what to think of Tony. It's my job to provide a fuller understanding of who he is and allow them to make up their own minds. Discernment was something that was really important for us to communicate: What you see is not always what you get.

You see it in episodes one and two. [Editor's note: Tony lives with his wife and a group of other women he refers to as his girlfriends.] There's a very specific mentality rooted in Red Pill philosophy, where the role of a man is to control these women and provide for them, but also to assert himself. He's the leader, and they must follow. I think one of the things Tony is always battling is that he presents in such a nice way and isn't aggressive like [his friend and fellow biohacking influencer] Leo was, but there's still this desire to control the women. The women are very strong, opinionated women.

From conversations with Tony during the making of this documentary, I know a lot of the women didn't realize they were coming into a harem. They thought they were his one and only true love, and then they've entered this environment and suddenly they're in competition with one another.

That competition is part of the dynamic of how the harem works. The way Tony puts it is that if they're in competition with one another, they try harder to vie for his attention, love, and affection. That's an incredibly complicated way of pitting women against each other, and somewhat dehumanizing.

What I want to be really careful of is that these aren't a bunch of outrageous, crazy people doing crazy things from the start. It actually begins in a real human place, a place all of us can relate to. I want to be the best version of myself. Yeah, of course I do. That's very relatable.

What happens within this is that some of the needs, in Elon [Muscular, one of Tony Huge’s mentees and a content creator]'s case, a sense of belonging, a father figure, all of those kinds of things that he's craving, aren't solved by taking one pill. These are really deep societal issues that are complex and need to be approached with a multidimensional complexity.

Therein lies a lot of the challenges with this world, because the extreme and the attention keep pushing those goalposts further. You get a bigger jawline, a bigger penis, bigger muscles, and you're still not feeling happy. I think it creates this kind of trap that some men can get stuck within, because the original solution was never going to solve that problem to begin with.

Honestly, it was really important for me to make this. A lot of my prior work has centered on women and diverse perspectives, and it's such an honor and privilege to do that kind of work. But I also recognize I was existing in a bit of an echo chamber, so doing this project took me well outside my comfort zone.

I use this example with kids: When they're scared at night, you shine a light in the room. You look under the bed, you shine a light into it, and it makes the thing that's inside your head less scary. There was a little bit of that in making this documentary, of really looking at it and understanding it, witnessing how people come in, why they stay, and why they also can't leave, and using those things as what I need to teach my son. I need to teach him discernment. I need to teach him the difference between a YouTube influencer who's performing and one who's actually giving genuine, real tips.

In this day and age, where clipping culture and soundbites matter, there's no room for context. We're in a post-truth era, and no one's taking the time to provide context, human dimension, or other perspectives. I want my son to understand how the internet and influencer culture work so he can make his own decisions with more critical thought than what's often taught in the public space.

Yeah, of course. I never wanted to make something that was just another echo chamber. I want this documentary to reach people deep in the heart of the masculinity influencer space. I want them to see it. Everyone's going to have a different reaction, but most importantly, people are talking, and that's what I care about. I need the conversation, the depth of the conversation. That's what this is designed to have.

It's interesting because that question has come up a few times. There does appear to be a turning of the tides. Even within Tony's own universe, his sense of relevancy has shifted. He went from being the most masculine man he could be to wearing eyeliner. It's all become a lot more fluid and therefore a lot more interesting.

I think there's a time we're living through where the power structures that have existed for the last decade are starting to break down. People aren't feeling connected to them anymore, or they certainly aren't serving their needs.

I hope we're at a time of reckoning and change, where people are recognizing that this isn't working. There's so much more awareness about the issues men are facing, and there are specific influencers who are the opposite kind, who are speaking about this stuff more. There are some incredible voices in this space starting to counter the other perspectives out there.

#6742. Richemont’s Jewelry Sales Rise 14%

Jewelry sales at Cartier’s parent company decelerated in fiscal Q2, after surging 24% in Q1. Jewelry maisons’ sales were up 14% to €4.4 billion in the second quarter of fiscal 2027, below consensus expectations of 16% growth, while Richemont posted group sales up 13% at constant exchange rates to €6 billion, above consensus expectations of 12%. The Richemont share price was down 6% in morning trading.

Sales at the specialty watchmakers division, including Piaget, IWC Schaffhausen and Jaeger-LeCoultre, rose 12%, smashing consensus expectations of 4% — a “major positive surprise”, as Bernstein analyst Luca Solca put it. Second-quarter sales in the conglomerate’s “other houses” division, which includes Chloé and Alaïa, were up 9%.

By geography, Richemont sales in the Americas were up 19% in Q2, Europe was up 15%, Asia-Pacific increased by 10%, and Japan rose by 23%. The Middle East and Africa were down 7%, significantly missing expectations of 4% growth.

China’s macro environment has been a major drag on luxury’s third-quarter earnings. Richemont was not immune to the challenges in the Mainland China market but is seeing growth in Greater China overall. “The confidence factor in mainland China is still not at its all-time high. We still see some rather soft business, although stable,” Richemont CEO Nicolas Bos said during a media call on Friday. “What’s interesting is that the trends in Greater China, particularly in Hong Kong and Macau, are extremely positive, so the Chinese clientele as a whole is really showing positive trends.”

Richemont chairman Johann Rupert, who was on the call, also noted the group’s difficulties in China. “ If anybody thinks we're less affected by [market conditions in] China, on the contrary. I’ll give you, for instance, Jaeger-LeCoultre is down 46% in China, yet 17% up for the year. So the rest of the world did so well that they could absorb China. Very good management and excellent products.”

Meanwhile, Alaïa has yet to appoint a new creative director following the departure of Pieter Mulier in March. Asked to comment on the timing for a successor appointment, Bos said: “The maison is doing very well. We have very good momentum and dynamics, and we had a beautiful presentation this September that was completely driven by the team in the studio, which was highly appreciated and successful. So we take our time. Alaïa is very much a maison that’s built on the long-term, and we believe there is a timeless style.” The executive declined to comment on speculation surrounding possible creative changes at Chloé.

Alexa Chung photographed for Chloé’s Resort 2027 campaign.

He also declined to comment on “any rumors that have to do with other companies” when asked to confirm Richemont’s involvement in discussions to join a consortium bidding for De Beers.

As British mining group Anglo American seeks to sell its 85% stake in De Beers, Bloomberg reported on October 15 that Richemont participated in talks.

Johann Rupert’s son,  Anton Rupert, participated in the earnings call for the first time since being appointed Richemont co-deputy chairman in September.  When asked during the media call when he will hand over his post to his son, Johann Rupert replied with a laugh: “Whenever I want to. Do you think I should?” He continued: “ I’m definitely not wedded to this. We’re having fun. I’m leaving a lot of decisions.”

Despite the slowdown, Richemont remains the best-in-class in this season’s earnings calendar. On why Richemont is doing so well, Johann Rupert said: “ That’s really due to already having handed over a lot to Nicolas [Bos], Louis Ferla at Cartier, and Anton [...]. The transitions have already taken place. Cartier, Van Cleef, and Jaeger-LeCoultre are run by different people. And maybe we’re doing better because we have a better system and a culture of collegiality[...].  And we have a pretty good idea where we’re going to be in three years’ time. That gives all of our colleagues a sense of purpose.”

Analysts had anticipated a decline in third-quarter growth, but the reality turned out worse than expected. LVMH reported a sales increase of 1% in Q3; Kering sales were down 1%. Meanwhile, Hermès sales were up 4.3%, the Prada brand reported sales up 1% and Miu Miu down 3%; the Moncler brand was down 1%; Burberry reported a 4% rise in second-quarter comparable store sales and the Zegna brand was up 8.2%.

“Richemont continues to be head and shoulders above the rest of the major luxury peers,” Bernstein’s Solca wrote in a note. “The recovery in profit margins on the back of lower gold prices and abating currency headwinds is particularly reassuring.”

#6741. What James Gunn’s Firing Means for the Future of DC Studios

For some reason, I foolishly believed they’d get it right this time. James Gunn’s Superman, which formally launched the DC cinematic universe he’s been masterminding alongside Peter Safran, was a refreshing take on a somewhat impenetrable character. I had some reservations about the rest of Gunn’s proposed slate—like following that movie with a Supergirl adventure, which proved to be every bit the misfire I imagined it would be—but bringing a contemporary Clark Kent to the screen was no small accomplishment. Gunn’s tone and his sensibility, I thought, might finally make way for the silver-screen Justice League adventure we deserved.

A silly hope, as proven by Monday’s big news: Gunn and Safran are out, in the wake of the WB-Paramount-Skydance unholy merger. Yet another auteur’s DC regime has been clipped before it could even find its footing. After the shock of the announcement wore off, my mind immediately went to that James Franco meme, the one where he’s about to be hanged. First time?

20 years ago, the idea that superhero C-listers like Iron Man and Thor would be at the top of the film adaptation pyramid while the stars of the Justice League toiled in a constant cycle of developmental destroy-and-rebuild would have been laughable. That’s part of what makes Kevin Feige’s MCU so impressive, of course: not just the scale and scope of his interconnected series of films, but doing it with a bunch of guys who were never all that popular in the larger superhero firmament. But as that regime rose, DC’s fortunes seesawed—with the Christopher Nolan Bat-trilogy as a beautiful outlier—and its fans have had to endure one indignity after another.

Us DC loyalists are basically like fans of the pre-2026 Knicks, or the pre-2004 Red Sox, or the pre-2016 Cavs—take your pick. I wouldn’t even call myself so hardcore, but those were the guys I grew up on, especially as more of a Saturday morning cartoon-watcher than a comics reader. Bruce Timm’s Batman and Superman animated series, the way those two shows dovetailed to make Justice League while also charting bold new territory with Batman Beyond—that was my jam. It was also the era of incredible Fox shows like Spider-Man and X-Men, but never did I think those two would continue to thrive while auteur after auteur tried and failed to do what Timm accomplished before a legion of appreciative 11-year-olds.

It goes back to Wolfgang Peterson’s aborted Batman versus Superman film, a Hollywood sliding doors moment that created the conditions under which a young, hungry Christopher Nolan could prove his blockbuster mettle with Batman Begins and give the greatest hero to ever do it a well-deserved cinematic reset. As Nolan’s stock rose, Bryan Singer’s attempt to restore ‘70s vibes with Superman Returns flopped almost immediately, leaving DC in a Highlander situation yet again. The goodwill Nolan generated with his trilogy gave way to what we came to know as the Snyderverse, starting with Zack Snyder’s Superman reset Man of Steel, a solid film that I could never bring myself to love wholeheartedly.

Historians will tell you it was shareholder thirst to compete with Marvel that spelled doom for Snyder—and the pressure to shoehorn Batman, Wonder Woman and the rest of their squad in to fast-track a Justice League movie. His era certainly cultivated a base of devoted, even rabid stans who will attack anyone who besmirches their leader’s genius. But personally, I spent all of those years in a state of disbelief about the way some of the genre’s sturdiest, best and most crowd-pleasing characters were being subjected to all of this Frank Miller-reject vibes: ultra slo-mo, fight scenes of wanton and artless destruction, not to mention the Gal Gadot line-readings and Bruce Wayne mowing bad guys down in between crossfit sessions. The illest superhero team to do it, in the hands of a guy who saw Jared Leto and thought, “There’s a guy who can succeed Heath Ledger as an Oscar-worthy villain.” Snyder’s step-down from Justice League after a family tragedy and seeing his vision superimposed with Joss Whedon’s was very undignified. But The SnyderCut? Still not for me.

James Gunn’s residency was the most promising thing to happen to the Justice gang in a while, at least for those of us who don’t chug Mountain Dew and listen to Eminem all day. He was the first director in a long time to really, truly understand Superman’s throwback optimistic essence and successfully repackage that for a contemporary audience. Forget about the larger DC universe—what Gunn built in Metropolis alone felt like the beginning of a beautiful universe. Corenswet’s affable take on the character paired with his chemistry with Rachel Brosnahan had me even hoping Gunn would ease up on the big picture and just luxuriate in more Superman adventures. Still, even his slate could only be so fresh: he started in the shadow of Matt Reeves and Robert Pattinson’s The Batman, a critically acclaimed reboot that didn’t square with his vision. At best, we were going to be subjected to the indelicate circumstance of having two different Batmen in production at once. (And that Gunn thought highly enough of Andy Muschietti’s The Flash to tap him for DCU’s Batman film was concerning, for sure.)

But he was building something, and he wasn’t wasting time. Even before he understandably stepped away for a family emergency, Reeves was taking his sweet time to get The Batman II off the ground; Gunn launched his Superman last July and intended to drop a sequel, Man of Tomorrow, next July, one that likely would’ve built up to a Justice League film a little more gracefully than Snyder was allowed to. He may have been indulging side quests a little too freely, green-lighting things like a spin-off series for Skyler Gisondo’s Jimmy Olsen, but his focus on the main play at hand never wavered. The narrative that he was meandering was always in bad faith; look no further than Superman's first act, which breathlessly goes about establishing the status quo of Gunn’s DCU at times to the script’s detriment.

We were already seeing those seeds planted: this past summer’s Lanterns series on HBO, for instance, through which Aaron Pierre managed to turn John Stewart into something closer to a household name hero. (Pierre and Adria Arjona, who is most likely playing Wonder Woman, were set to appear in Man of Tomorrow.) Gunn’s quippy, vibrant vision may not have been for everyone, but he at least deserved the chance to cook a little bit longer. In a weird way, Gunn’s firing feels like one of the first pushbacks to the midterms blue wave. Looking for politics in comic book fare is ultimately asinine, but there’s a reason Superman 2025 was one of the most meme'd movies during the post November 3rd wave of optimism, to say nothing of the movie's plot being a paper-thin allegory for Israel and Palestine.

So what happens now? Who knows. Man of Tomorrow might be released as a sort of post-mortem, or it could be shelved altogether. Does David Corenswet go the way of Brandon Routh? Have we seen the last of this iteration of John Stewart? Will Adria Arjona’s Wonder Woman even get off the ground?

We’re back to square one. Skydance head David Ellision has already replaced Gunn and Safran with ex-MCU producer Jeremy Latcham, a guy who’s more concerned about making movies that’ll play for meemaw, peepaw and the reverend. It appears he'll be a down-the-middle role player who can serve up the most basic, populist take on all of these adaptations. I’m giving up on ever seeing a coherent, let alone genuinely great take on this squad of heroes. Many have tried, all have failed, and the people in charge have only gotten dumber. Go with God, DC faithful. We’ll always have the Bruce Timm cartoons.

#6740. Christy Turlington’s Ruby-Red Lipstick Is the Easy Makeup Secret for Women Over 40

Shop our favorite creamy, hydrating, and smoothing lipstick formulas

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

The last few years have been marked by the “Lip Balm Wars.” That is, every brand—from Hailey Bieber’s Rhode to prestige labels like Chanel and Dior—has launched more sheer, glossy, and hydrating formulas than classic lipstick bullets. But even though we all own more than 10 emotional-support lip balms in various shades, flavors, and finishes, there's still nothing more powerful than a statement-making lip. This is especially true for women over 40.

Last night, supermodel Christy Turlington stepped out at the Museum of Modern Art’s 2026 Annual Film Benefit in New York, wearing a knit dress from Matthieu Blazy’s fall 2026 Chanel collection. A dress this graphic and eye-catching needs makeup to balance it, and Turlington paired it with black eyeliner and a glossy ruby-red lipstick.

While we don’t know the exact shade she wore last night, it’s clearly a formula that sits somewhere between a satin lipstick and a gloss-balm, with pigment that doesn’t sacrifice moisture or shine. Turlington is a Lancôme ambassador, so it could be the brand’s Lip Idole Butterglow Hydrating Lip Balm or L’Absolu Rouge Cream Lipstick. Otherwise, Chanel makes a gorgeous option in both the Rouge Coco Flash and Rouge Allure Extrait formulas. These formulas subtly plump and moisturize dry lips while blurring lip lines and imperfections.

Lancôme L'Absolu Rouge Moisturizing Cream Lipstick in 397 Berry Noir

Chanel Hydrating Vibrant Shine Lip Colour

Lancome Lip Idole Squalane-12 Butterglow Hydrating Lip Balm

The best part of this look is that it proves you don’t need to match your lipstick exactly to your outfit, as long as they’re in the same color family. While the Chanel dress is more of an orange-red knit, Turlington’s lipstick is a more neutral ruby that harmonizes with the warm tones and shades in the rest of her look. Plus, raspberry or ruby-red lipstick can brighten your face in seconds, even with little to no other makeup.

Bold lipstick is a bit outside Turlington’s day-to-day comfort zone; she told Bazaar recently that she’s “definitely an old-school Carmex or ChapStick kind of person, because I’m constantly reapplying it to my dry lips, especially in the winter.” The rest of her routine is equally as effortless: “I wash my face in the morning and moisturize a lot. Sometimes I even double-moisturize because, especially at this time of year, I get dry skin. And then, I’ll add a nice little layer of foundation, some blush, and mascara, and that’s kind of it, I’m on my way.”

#6739. Ferrari Spring 2027 Ready-to-Wear

In the same way that a lover of Louis Vuitton luggage may want to dine at an LV-branded cafe, or a Dior addict may want to rest their head on a Dior pillow on a Dior bed at a Dior hotel, why wouldn’t an aficionado of Ferrari sportscars not want to wear a plush jacket or a sleek pair of pants from the Italian automobile company?

“Look at what Louis Vuitton is doing—they are becoming the first sponsor at F1,” says Rocco Iannone, creative director of Ferrari’s ready-to-wear collection. “They are too big to sell only small leather goods and bags. So they need to enlarge their experiences.”

“Luxury,” he added, “is becoming very multidimensional.”

Iannone was at Ferrari’s newly opened Soho boutique, in a former Nespresso space directly opposite the Prada store (all three brands are Italian icons, in their own way, if you think about it). The store is all sinuous lines of burnished steel, evoking the monumentality of a Richard Serra sculpture, set off against concrete, glass, and leather. Downstairs is the brand’s more commercial collection, with a stand of logo baseball caps and small accessories like pens and keychains on display, plus a collaboration with Swizz Beatz, the kind of Ferrari owner who has to pause and go through a mental checklist when you ask him how many cars he owns from the company. Upstairs, the recent runway collection hangs by a table where shoppers can customize their Ferrari-shaped bags (to match their own, a common request), plus a curtained-off space for VIPs.

A few days later, the brand held the show for its latest collection in a downtown gallery. “America’s the most important market for us,” said John Elkann, the brand’s chief executive, before the show. “And [Ferrari] is very intertwined with America—there is no better place to be than here in New York.” Alongside the runway were oversize tapestries that recreated the covers of a magazine the company once produced with the textile manufacturer Rubelli, in vibrant shades, including, of course, the fiery Ferrari red.

On the runway were creamy tailored pieces with a subtle rippling effect, slouchy tracksuits, slick leather skirts and cropped bombers, and body-hugging intarsia knits in swirling, sometimes chaotic patterns, that evoked either marble or the busy branding on a race car driver’s uniform. It closed with a passage of lush pieces in mocha brown, where denim “melted” into a leather printed to look like turtle shells—something Iannone was particularly pleased with—or lighter silks with a puckered appearance.

In recent seasons, Iannone has mellowed the more dynamic, in-your-face aesthetic he launched with—all those graphic hits of neon and showy logos!—but in doing so, has lost some of the flashy, swaggering bravado that’s foundational to the brand. Ferrari is sleek, sexy, and ostentatious in its desire for speed and excitement. This collection was reserved and tasteful, but it missed the visceral, gutsy element that makes Ferrari—and fashion, for that matter—roar like an engine.

#6736. Denis Villeneuve Talks ‘Dune: Part Three’ and Rebooting James Bond: ‘We Cannot F*ck It Up.’

“I’m out of a job,” Denis Villeneuve said, jokingly. Hours earlier, Villeneuve had signed off on the IMAX 70-milimeter print of Dune: Part Three, officially wrapping post-production on that film—and in turn, a decade-long chapter of the Quebecois writer-director’s working life.

Fresh off this milestone, Villeneuve and GQ had come to the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art in Los Angeles for a conversation and a private screening of Dune: Part Two, presented by OMEGA, in honor of his anointment as GQ’s Director of the Year. Global Editorial Director Adam Baidawi introduced Villeneuve before the director and GQ’s Zach Baron dove into a conversation that covered his original Dune plans, where Dune: Part Three breaks from its predecessors, and Villeneuve’s feelings about taking over the James Bond franchise.

GQ’s Adam Baidawi and Zach Baron with Denis Villeneuve

“I feel light,” the director of the year told Baron, then added, “Numb.” He was still processing Dune’s end, he said—while also coming to grips with closing the book on “the most rewarding, inspiring, and best ten years of my life as a filmmaker.”

Villeneuve’s first two Dune films have raked in more than a billion dollars at the box office. Part Three appears likely to nearly double that when it hits theaters (and locks up most of the world’s IMAX screens) a week before Christmas. But at one point during his conversation with Baron, the director pushed back gently on the notion of these movies as a “franchise.”

“There was nothing industrial in the way they were made,” Villeneuve said. They were the work of “a bunch of friends”—a familial crew, out in the desert putting things together.

“In French,” the Quebecois director continued, “there is a word—artisanal. They are very personal. Made with a lot of care. They’re little big things—but in a way, they are delicate.”

After all, as sprawling and cosmically grand as they are, these movies are also a deeply personal project for the director, born of images that took root in his head when he first read Frank Herbert’s thick-as-a-brick, notoriously adaptation-resistant 1965 novel Dune at age 13. Later, as Villeneuve racked up credits and clout, people would ask him what his dream project was; the answer was always Dune.

“I kept saying to myself, Someone else will do it one day,” he told Baron. “Another filmmaker will adapt this book again. And I kept waiting, and I kept waiting, until I felt ready to do it myself.”

Herbert wrote five escalatingly bonkers Dune sequels before his death in 1986, but Villeneuve intended to walk away from the table after adapting the first book across two films.

“Trilogies are very dangerous,” he told Baron. “The first movie is a promise, and if you fulfill the promise with the second one, then there’s a feeling of security that comes with that, and you feel that you have a recipe…That’s the trap. Because then you repeat yourself.”

But after wrapping Part Two, Villeneuve found himself unable to stop thinking about Dune Messiah—the second Dune novel, which Herbert supposedly wrote in frustration, believing the audience had missed the point by embracing Paul Atreides as a hero.

Villeneuve said his take on Messiah is “a different beast” than the first two films, built it around the tension between Timothée Chalamet’s Paul and his Fremen consort Chani (Zendaya), who Villeneuve has re-imagined—in a pivotal departure from Herbert’s version—as a nonbeliever who takes a critical view of Paul’s rise to power.

Neel Shah, Timothy Simons, and Michael Lasker

Of course, the specter (S.P.E.C.T.R.E.?) of another franchise hung over the proceedings at the Lucas Museum. Villeneuve, after all, is only technically between jobs; he’s a self-described “monomaniac” who insists that he can only hyper-focus on one project at a time and has been locked in on Dune for a decade, but the as-yet-untitled 26th Bond film is in motion, with Villeneuve signed on to direct.

GQ’s Adam Baidawi, Denis Villeneuve, and OMEGA’s Lucien Jornod

He could say almost nothing in public about the project, or even when he’d begin shooting it—he joked about having “the target of the sniper” on his chest—but spoke of feeling the responsibility not to fail: “We cannot fuck it up. We do not have the choice.”

Over the past week, the casting rumors around Villeneuve’s Bond reboot have reached what our UK colleagues accurately termed the “fever-dream” stage. It might be Callum Turner or Slow Horses’ Jack Lowden, but it might be Robert Pattinson, who’s emerged as a surprise front-runner after months of supposition about the part being earmarked for a relative unknown. At some point, toward the end of Tuesday’s conversation, the subject of Bond 26’s lead could no longer be avoided.

“Has the role of James Bond been cast?” Baron asked the director.

“It’s—it’s in the process. In the process,” Villeneuve said with a smile. “I am pushing the gas.”

“Blink once for Robert Pattinson,” Baron suggested, “and twice for Callum Turner.”

Villeneuve, for the record, did not blink. ✦

GQ would like to thank Legendary Entertainment, Warner Bros., and Brianna Smith.

#6735. Elias Matso Is the Twisted Corsetier Dressing Sydney Sweeney and Jenna Ortega

The young designer talked to Bazaar about craftsmanship, fittings, and developing his signature technique

These days, Elias Matso is known for twisted corsetry worn by the likes of Sydney Sweeney and Jenna Ortega. But the first time he noticed the impact of a good costume, he was a kid watching Julie Andrews in Victor/Victoria. He sat by the TV watching the Oscar-winning actor perform “Le Jazz Hot!” in Art Deco gowns, decadent headpieces, and dramatic feathered capes. “I know she was acting in that scene, but I just felt like she was so happy to be wearing those costumes,” he tells Harper’s Bazaar. “And I was obsessed with that.”

Matso is now 24, and it’s easy to see the impact of that moment on his creative approach. A recent graduate of Polimoda in Florence with Charles James, Bob Mackie, Mugler, and Mr. Pearl on his mood board, he crafts avant-garde, couture corsetry. (It’s perhaps no surprise that he has a history of making costumes for drag performers.) His approach is personal and intimate, rooted in hand craftsmanship and collaborative dialogue with clients.

In October 2025, Sweeney made waves when she wore a crystal naked dress, pulled from Christian Cowan’s Spring/Summer 2026 collection and made in collaboration with the young designer. The piece featured twisted corsetry and a semi-sheer body that hugged the Euphoria star’s body—and, naturally, the public had quite a lot to say about it. “I did not anticipate that it would be as big as it was,” the artist admits. “It was really cool that the conversation left fashion and became a bigger conversation about women’s bodies and what modesty should look like or shouldn’t look like. And how a lot of the world doesn’t know what boobs look like.”

While the discourse surprised Matso, it reflected one of his own core beliefs: that “fashion is at least 50% the person who’s wearing the thing.” He keeps this in mind during fittings, ensuring clients feel comfortable and beautiful every step of the way. Below, he talks to Bazaar about his early references, his focus on craftsmanship, and the colorful steel-boning dress recently worn by Jenna Ortega.

As a kid, I had a paper doll of myself, and whenever there were clothes that I wanted that I didn’t have, I would make them for the paper doll. It was pocket sized, and whenever I was bored—which was all the time, because I have attention deficit issues—I would pull it out and play.

It is. It was my third year and I wanted to explore the tension that children hold, when they feel like they’re growing faster than they can keep up with, and feeling at odds with themselves, because that’s how I felt when I was a kid. There was this feeling, especially in the queer world, of being pulled in different directions, gender-wise. And so I had developed that idea, and then through sketching and conversations with my teachers, we started getting more and more towards this very literal idea of a twist. And then the collaboration that I did with Christian Cowan pushed it further.

I was in New York over the summer before my senior year, and I was looking for jobs and not getting anything. I started looking into scooping ice cream at Van Leeuwen’s and stuff like that. And then, one day, I got a text from Alicia Keys’s stylist and a DM from Christian that was like, “Do you want to do some dresses for my show?” It was a good day.

It actually wasn’t originally supposed to be that fabric. We couldn’t find the fabric we wanted, and we couldn’t figure out how to put as many stones as we needed onto the fabric that we found. Then we just found this sheer fabric, and we were like, “Okay, it’s going to be the original dress, but it’s going to be completely see-through.”

I made it to fit this gorgeous six-foot-tall model from Finland. And this is why fit is so fun, because with that dress, there was this miracle where it fit her so perfectly one way, and then it fit Sydney, who has completely different proportions, in this totally other, also beautiful way. Often when things get pulled from a runway, they don’t fit like that. And it was just really cool to see.

I really like meeting people in person when I can because it just always creates a better outcome. I feel like the conversation is so much about your personality, but also your physiology, the way you’re built and the way you’re made up. People’s bodies respond differently. So it’s really important to do fittings and to check in with people before, during, and after the fitting, and ask, “How intense of an experience do you want this to be? What will make you feel the most beautiful, the most comfortable?”

Sometimes a little bit of discomfort is part of being comfortable, but you have to have signed up for that. That’s my thing that I’ve learned: Discomfort, if you’re prepared, can be part of it. But there has to be a conversation if discomfort is involved, or else we are forgetting that fashion is at least 50% the person who’s wearing the thing.

When I start a collection, I’m always looking through the archives of a museum, like the Whitney or often the Guggenheim, because you have less control over what you’re going to find. [For this piece,] I had found one painting that led me to Mark Ranger’s website. And we got in touch and then collaborated the whole year. It turns out we explore a lot of the same themes. Here, the dress was supposed to be about time and our body’s relationship to gravity and this idea of melting, not in a way that we’re trying to resist and slow down, but in a way that’s just natural and beautiful.

The goal was to make something unrecognizable, but using recognizable techniques. I already had a lot of steel boning because it’s the same stuff that’s inside all these corsets. And so I just got more, and then I started chopping it up into smaller and smaller pieces. I was able to create a relationship with Preciosa, who does crystals for a lot of big brands—I met them through a trip that they did to my school. I just came up with this weird technique that was, I guess, a test of my own physical and mental strength in a way.

I didn’t make it with Jenna in mind. I never thought it would have all these different lives and stages.

I guess I’m seeing it less and less valued in fashion. And even when something is hand-done and comes out gorgeous and successful, the people that wind up getting the praise for those things are not the people who do the thing, but the people who have curated those artisans—the artistic directors, the designers. My friends and I have just graduated, we’re looking for work, and I see my friends who have really singular skills getting so undervalued for their work and their time. That is something that is really frustrating to me. And in an age where so many things can be falsified via technology and the internet, I think things that you can’t fake are how something’s made, how something stands up over time, how something feels on the inside when you put it on. And designers care less and less about that, I guess.

I’m in a transitional stage where I’m not sure what I’m gonna do next. Every day, I get people asking me to make dresses on this scale for free or for bafflingly low amounts of money. You know, I’m told all the time that there’s no budget for things. People want couture for no budget. People in this industry have no shame when it comes to asking for that. For emerging designers, there are so many of us that they know that if I can’t supply what they’re looking for, they will find another independent designer who has the resources or the funds or the ability to provide that thing for less than what it’s worth. I do worry about that. But this press is making me think that maybe there is a niche for something that walks the line between art and fashion and not in the aesthetic sense, which people talk about all the time, but in the financial and logistical sense. So that’s what I’m trying to figure out.

Also, I found that if people are asking for things for free, it’s very rarely the client themselves. It’s often their team. I love the art of styling, but that is another reason that I find one-on-one relationships and conversations with the person who you’re going to be dressing really important. It makes them understand the level of attention or care that they are interacting with.

This is still in process, but I’m working on a piece with Laverne Cox. I always wanted to work with her. And then starting to work with her, I was like, “I was right.” Because she has such appreciation and respect for the process of everything and the details and how everything works. She’s a really respectful and engaging patron, and we’ve had a lot of interesting conversations about the designers that we both look up to.

For me, I want to take the momentum that I have and do something that feels exciting with it. And at the same time, I am not sure that I have the experience to start a company, you know? I am in conversations with lots of people who I’ve always wanted to collaborate with, and it’s so exciting. Really, really exciting and mind-blowing. And at the same time, I’m reaching out to brands that I admire to see what openings they have because we all need stability. I’m trying to remain as flexible as possible.

#6734. Hunter Schafer Gives Daryl Hannah’s Iconic ‘Blade Runner’ Beauty a 2099 Update

For the premiere of a show set in 2099, Hunter Schafer went all the way back to 1982. Attending the Los Angeles premiere of Blade Runner 2099 last night, the actor delivered a striking, menacing android beauty homage to Ridley Scott’s original sci-fi classic.

“The concept was a nod to Daryl Hannah’s character Pris in the original Blade Runner movie,” makeup artist Sandy Ganzer confirms to Vogue. “Her makeup is so iconic and we wanted to pay homage with a modern and more red carpet-friendly version of it.”

Hannah’s punkish replicant is responsible for one of cinema’s most enduring beauty looks. We first got to know Pris with a shock of peroxide-blonde hair and a dramatic, amask-like strip of shadow across the eyes. For Schafer, Ganzer reimagined that graphic eye makeup in metallic gunmetal and smoky taupe, extending the shadow horizontally toward the temples and across the bridge of the nose for that cyborg look.

To create the shape, Ganzer began with the matte grayish-brown crease shade from the Natasha Denona Glam palette, layering its deepest metallic gunmetal shadow over the top for depth and dimension. She then applied the white highlighter from Dior’s Universal Glow palette along the bridge of Schafer’s nose, fading it into the inner corners of her eyes for a futuristic, silvered glow. Prada Beauty eyeliner and mascara created more precise definition. The secret to that razor-sharp upper edge? “I cleaned up the edges on top with a Q-tip dipped in micellar water to make sure it was ultra sharp and left the bottom edges diffused and blurry,” Ganzer explains.

The rest of the face was kept deliberately soft, with a little Haus Labs foundation and concealer, the lightest touch of Saie blush in Mia, and Lancôme’s Hush Hush lip color, dabbed on with a finger for a romantic and blurred finish. It was a necessary contrast to the severity of the eyes.

Daryl Hannah as Pris in Ridley Scott’s Blade Runner.

“We really wanted the eyes to have their own moment, so with the hair, I wanted to keep it feeling a bit more restrained against all the glamour,” hairstylist Rena Calhoun explains. Schafer’s hair was pulled back into a deliberately disheveled updo, with flyaways and loose pieces escaping at the back. “The idea was for it to feel a bit rough and undone, with little pieces falling out in the back that gave it a slightly messy, frazzled quality, almost like Pris’s texture in the film.”

Styled by Dara, Schafer kept up the dystopian femmebot look in a burnt brown-and-black leather Prada corset dress with a sculptural neckline, layered beneath a voluminous chocolate-brown fur coat, with textured black tights and sparkling earrings.

Method-glamming has very much been amped up across the last year, thanks in part to Schafer’s Euphoria co-star Zendaya. Out on the press tour for The Odyssey, Zendaya swapped her bixie for ethereal, Greek goddess lengths care of hairstylist Coree Moreno. They had lots of fun with Grecian half-up half-down styles and braided crowns.

Schafer stars in the forthcoming Prime Video series, which picks up 50 years after the events of Blade Runner 2049. She plays Cora, a human fugitive who assumes the identity of a Blade Runner within the LAPD to protect her younger brother and secure a future for humanity. Alongside Michelle Yeoh, who plays a replicant nearing the end of her life, Schafer finds herself navigating a dystopian Los Angeles in which the boundaries between human and machine have become increasingly precarious.

And if this premiere is any indication, the Blade Runner 2099 press tour is shaping up to be a particularly thrilling beauty and fashion ride. Schafer and Allen have already been exploring the possibilities of sci-fi dressing, from a graphic, color-blocked Prada look to a neon, crystal-embellished NIHL ensemble. There is certainly plenty of aesthetic territory to explore in the Blade Runner universe itself, oscillating from the cyberpunk heroines to more noir glamour. With Hunter Schafer at the controls, 2099 is already looking rather good.

#6732. Colored Tights Are Taking Over—Here’s How Fashion Girls Are Styling Them Now

Consider this your sign to swap basic black for cobalt, red, lavender, and more.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

’Tis the season to cozy up, which means it’s also the season to have a little fun with tights. This year, try swapping out the traditional black hose and elevate your outfits with a pop of color instead. The colored tights renaissance was alive and well on the fall 2026 runways, with Chanel, Marc Jacobs, and Valentino leading the charge.

Off the runway, the street style crowd has been just as enthusiastic, livening up their looks with bold tights. If you need outfit inspiration, we’ve rounded up the best ways fashion girls are styling colorful hosiery right now.

And when in doubt, let the tights do the talking: pair a bold, colorful pair with a neutral base of black, gray, or brown, and you can’t go wrong.

Below, check out some elevated ways to style colorful tights this season.
